athletes.name: Valentina Pistritto
notes: Valentina is from Palermo in Sicily, lives in Geneva, and works as a Procurement Officer for the United Nations.
She has loved going underwater since she was a child — she just did not know it was a sport back then.
She is also a mum — hello to her daughter Isabella, thirteen years old.
And she recently took up sport shooting — pistols and rifles — to work on focus and concentration.
UN officer, mum, shooter, freediver.
Valentina does not do things by half.
Shoutouts to brother Antonio who is here today, coach Ivan, and depth coach Riccardo.

athletes.name: Hannah Nicol
notes: World Championship experience, a DYNB of 159 metres, a DYN of 150 metres, instructor credentials, safety diver experience — Hannah brings everything to the pool and performs at every level of the sport.
Eindhoven 2025 was a strong outing for her, and she is back to do it again.

transition: Short break — and then straight back into it.

athletes.name: Eric Gerritsma
notes: Eric Gerritsma is the second Dutch Eric in the pool today — and he has earned his own introduction!
A DYN personal best of 150 metres, and he is here to swim it again.
Let's go Eric!

athletes.name: Roeland Maes
notes: Ten competitions, and Roeland just keeps getting better.
His bi-fins best is 166 metres, no-fins 125 metres — strong numbers across the board.
Belgium has a lot of great athletes today, and Roeland is right at the heart of that team.

transition: Our next athletes are stepping up. Let's welcome them.

athletes.name: Danny Martherus
notes: Danny is a psychiatric nurse from Zeist in the Netherlands and trains at Freediving Utrecht.
He calls himself a generalist — in his job, in his sports, in life.
Freediving is his weekly mindful moment — thirty-one competitions in, and he still finds calm at the bottom of the pool.
He says hi to everyone.
Hi Danny! 🖖

athletes.name: Brieuc Simon
notes: Five competitions and already a bi-fins best of 150 metres and no-fins at 134 metres.
Brieuc is moving fast up the Belgian rankings and shows no sign of slowing down.
Today could be another big step forward.

transition: Every athlete here trained for this moment. Full attention.

athletes.name: Jurgen Reinderink
notes: Canada, the Philippines, Latvia, the Netherlands — Jurgen has competed on nearly every continent and brought his bi-fins best of 179 metres and no-fins of 140 metres to each of them.
Judge, instructor, athlete.
Thirteen competitions in and still going strong.

athletes.name: Zakaria Brahmi
notes: Zakaria is Algeria's number one in the pool — and he earned that title the hard way.
A national record of 161 metres in dynamic fins is a big, big number.
Three competitions in and already this good?
We cannot wait to see what comes next.

transition: While our athletes take their final breaths — give them a big hand.

athletes.name: Flynn Thomas
notes: Flynn is from Cornwall, where he surfs and skydives when he is not holding his breath.
He says there is something very addictive about freediving — he still has no idea why he started.
He has one message for his teammate Chris Burtwell — 'Tell Chris I am coming for him.'
Big thanks to George and Daan from Aquacity Freediving — the most supportive people he could ask for.

athletes.name: Chris Burtwell
notes: Chris is from Cornwall in England and works as a farrier — he shoes horses for a living.
He is also a dad of two.
Nine competitions in, DYN of 175 metres, DYNB of 173 metres.
Shoutouts to coaches Georgina Miller and Daan Verhoeven.
And Flynn Thomas has a message for him.
Chris — you have been warned.

transition: Next heat coming up. Give our athletes a moment to focus.

athletes.name: Sam Mccullen
notes: Eleven competitions, four gold medals, a World Championship in Japan, and one of the busiest competition schedules in the British team.
His no-fins best of 154 metres is a seriously impressive number.
Sam shows up everywhere and performs everywhere — a fantastic competitor.

athletes.name: Anni Højgaard
notes: Anni is from the Faroe Islands, competing for Denmark, and trains with the Pearl Divers club in Holbaek.
By day she works in health care and nursing.
She says freediving gives her one thing above everything else — me time.
Ten gold medals, eighteen competitions, and she still just wants a quiet moment underwater.
Shoutouts to her teammates Valentina and Michele — who are also in this pool today.

transition: A few seconds to breathe — for us and for them.

athletes.name: Darryl Palmer
notes: Darryl is from Hertfordshire and trains in a small 18-metre pool with his partner Paige as his safety diver.
She does not even freedive.
By day he invests in data centres — and when he is not doing that, he is boxing or climbing mountains.
His reason for the sport: the glide.
Nothing else feels like it.
Thanks to coach Theo-Patrick Fourcade, and of course to Paige, who makes it all possible.

athletes.name: Valentin Sadan
notes: Static six twenty-one, dynamic 200 metres, bi-fins 177 metres, no-fins 137 metres — Valentin has no weak spot.
He works for a luxury hotel and travel company and lives just around the corner from his training pool in London.
Very convenient.
He says freediving is the most addictive activity he can think of.
Thanks to coach Vincent at Hack Your Breath and partner Preeya.

transition: The pool is quiet for now. Not for long.

athletes.name: Joost Rothweiler
notes: Dutch national records in both dynamic fins at 209 metres and bi-fins at 217 metres.
Seven gold medals.
And today he swims at home in front of a home crowd.
Joost is the favourite in the finswimming lanes, and everyone in this pool knows it.
This one is special.

athletes.name: Martin Sung Jensen
notes: Denmark's national record holder in both DYN at 252 metres and DYNB — that puts him world number 38 in the monofin and world number 70 in bi-fins.
A static best of seven minutes eight seconds confirms this is someone who is very comfortable sitting in the dark.
He also holds his own in no-fins — 154 metres, national number eleven.
Two gold medals, a silver, and a bronze — he collects hardware across every pool discipline he enters.
Most recently out at the Swedish National Pool Championships in March, so he arrives here sharp and race-ready.
Denmark's strongest pool athlete today — and one of the top thirty-eight in the world.

transition: Every heat, a different story. Let's see what this one brings.
